passages.t: The mountains of Israel will bear fruit again
passages.happening:
God speaks to the mountains of Israel. The nations have mocked them and seized them as their own, and Edom above all (verses 2-5). Now God swears that the nations will bear their own shame (verse 7). ‘But you, O mountains of Israel, will produce branches and bear fruit for My people Israel, for they will soon come home’ (verse 8). The land will be tilled and sown, its towns rebuilt and its people multiplied (verses 9-11).

Then God explains why Israel was scattered. They defiled the land by their ways and their idols (verses 16-18). And wherever they went, they profaned his holy name, because the nations said of them that they were the LORD's people and yet had to leave his land (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
These oracles belong to the years after Jerusalem's fall. Judah was emptied, many towns lay in ruins, and neighbors, Edom especially, had moved into its southern lands.

The exiles faced a crisis of faith as sharp as the political one. In the ancient world a nation's defeat was taken as its god's defeat. So the nations said that the LORD's people had been thrown out of his land, as if he could not keep them.

Verse 17 compares Israel's conduct to the uncleanness of a woman's monthly period, which sounds harsh to modern ears. Under Israel's purity laws that uncleanness was not a sin; it meant a time of separation from holy things. Ezekiel, a priest, uses it to say that Israel's sins made the land unfit for God's presence.
passages.later: Leviticus said the land would vomit out a people who defiled it (Leviticus 18:28). The psalm laments that the nations ask, ‘Where is their God?’ (Psalm 79:10).
passages.asks: God promised that the mountains would bear fruit again for a people who had not yet come home. Ask what ruins in your life you have given up on. And ask what it would mean to hope that God can make them fruitful.

passages.t: A new heart and a new spirit
passages.happening:
‘It is not for your sake that I will act, O house of Israel, but for My holy name’ (verse 22). God will show the holiness of his great name before the nations (verse 23). He will gather Israel from the nations and bring them home (verse 24).

‘I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean. I will cleanse you from all your impurities and all your idols’ (verse 25). ‘I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh’ (verse 26). ‘And I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes’ (verse 27). ‘You will be My people, and I will be your God’ (verse 28).

They will remember their ways and loathe themselves, and know that God acted for his own name (verses 31-32). People will say, ‘This land that was desolate has become like the garden of Eden’ (verse 35), and the ruined cities will be filled with people like flocks at a festival (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
The cleansing draws on priestly practice. Water was sprinkled to purify people from contact with death, and sprinkling marked people and objects as clean and set apart.

In the ancient world the heart was the center of thought, will and moral choice, not mainly of feeling. A heart of stone is a mind and will that cannot respond. A heart of flesh is alive and able to answer God. In chapter 18 God told the people to make themselves a new heart; here he promises to give it.

The return from Babylon began about fifty years later, after Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC. The returning community rebuilt the temple and resettled parts of Judah, a real fulfillment of the promise of rebuilt cities.
passages.later: Jeremiah heard the same promise: ‘I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts’ (Jeremiah 31:33). Moses had said, ‘The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts’ (Deuteronomy 30:6).
passages.hard:
Who is this promise for: the Jews who returned from Babylon, the church, or a future restoration of Israel?

Christians read the chapter in several ways, and this site takes no side. Almost all agree that the return from Babylon after 539 BC was a real first fulfillment of the promise to rebuild the ruins, and that the returned community did not yet have the new heart the chapter describes. Many interpreters, especially in Reformed and covenant traditions, see the promise of cleansing and the Spirit fulfilled in the new covenant community of Jews and Gentiles in Christ, with the land promise widened into the renewed creation. Dispensational interpreters, and others who expect a future national restoration of Israel, often reading Romans 11 alongside this chapter, hold that the promise will also be fulfilled for the Jewish people, including in the land. Jewish interpreters read it as God's pledge to the Jewish people that still awaits completion.

These are second-order questions among Christians. The chapter makes no claim about any modern state or border, and it stays focused on what all readers share: God will act for his name, and the new heart is his gift.
passages.asks: God gives the new heart his people could not make for themselves. Ask where you have been trying to change yourself by effort alone. And ask God, in the words of the psalm, to create a clean heart in you.
